chunks: This issue has no disagreement among the Muslims, and there is consensus that the obligation of Hajj is a single payment. We have included some of the narrations regarding this in our Great Book, and therefore we have not included them here.
1. As for what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Sinan from Hudhayfah ibn Mansur from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
God, the Mighty and Majestic, made Hajj obligatory upon the wealthy every year.
2. From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abu Jarir al-Qummi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Hajj is obligatory upon the wealthy every year.
3. And Ali ibn Ja'far narrated from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
Indeed, God the Exalted made Hajj obligatory upon the wealthy every year.

And this is His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: 'And to God belongs the pilgrimage to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it.' And whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is free of need of the worlds.
He said: I said, 'And whoever among us does not perform Hajj has disbelieved?' He said: 'No, but whoever says that this is not so has disbelieved.'

Therefore, the interpretation of these narrations is one of two things: either they are to be understood as recommending (mustahabb) rather than obligatory (fard/wajib), or the meaning is that for every year, in the manner of substitution (badal), because whoever upon whom Hajj became obligatory in the first year and did not perform it, it becomes obligatory upon him in the second year, and likewise if he did not perform it in the second year, it becomes obligatory upon him in the third year. And thus is the ruling for every year until he performs it, and it was not meant that he is obligated in every year in the manner of repetition.
ai.seo_question: Is Hajj obligatory every year for the wealthy in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction between narrations stating Hajj is obligatory annually for the wealthy and the consensus of a single obligation by interpreting 'every year' as a continuous duty of substitution until performed. This interpretation aligns with the principle that the obligation persists year after year if the initial opportunity is missed, rather than requiring multiple distinct performances. The text further distinguishes this from disbelief, noting that denying the obligation itself constitutes kufr, while merely failing to perform it does not.
